Every step has pointed at the same thing: a structure (Temporality, Spatiality, and Physicality together) that cannot fail to exist. That structure is what the book means by Nature. So at the level of necessity, Reality and Nature are the same thing, with no neutral ground outside the Conditions from which things could have been otherwise. One rival is still left standing, something transcendent alongside Nature, and that is taken up in Chapters 5 and 6.

Each step contributes one piece: the global modal status of possibility is fixed (§2.1); change is possible (§2.2); its possibility is necessary (§2.3); that necessity requires Temporality, Spatiality, and Physicality (§§2.4–2.5); the three are one change-realizing structure (§2.6); and there is no empty alternative beneath it (§2.7). Read together, they do not merely constrain what Reality could be: they identify its necessary structural content.

One identity bridge remains. Necessary co-instantiation alone would permit the thought that Reality has Nature as an endowment while remaining something more. Maximality and the available grounding positions close that remainder.

::: {.argument}
**The Reality–Nature Identity** · *The Grounding Trilemma*

1. Reality is the whole within which any real content belongs (§1.1).
1. Every real state, item, or world instantiates the necessary structural Conditions (§2.5). Anything real is therefore a configuration within Nature, not an item standing outside its conditions of reality.
1. Let G be a proposed additional ground of Nature. G must either ground Nature, be grounded by Nature, or stand in no grounding relation to Nature (§1.5.5).
1. If G grounds Nature, the grounding relation is directed, differentiates ground from grounded, and obtains as a real dependence. At role-resolution it reinstantiates T, S, and Φ; the alleged outside ground is already within the structure it grounds (§2.2.2).
1. If G is grounded by Nature, G is derivative within Nature. If G stands in no grounding relation to Nature, it is not an additional ground of Nature.
1. Therefore no real content or grounding office remains outside Nature. Structurally, Reality and Nature coincide: R = N.

:::

The result closes the modal-structural identity needed here: everything real is conditioned by Nature, and no additional ground occupies an exterior grounding position.

The whole line, from the chapter's first move to its last:

::: {.argument}
**Necessity of Nature** · *The Whole Line*

1. *Necessary Possibility (T1).* Real possibility ranges over one fixed domain W, so whatever is possible is necessarily possible. ◇P → □◇P. (§2.1)
1. *Cartesian Certainty.* The act of doubt is itself a change, so change is actual and therefore possible. ◇C. (§2.2)
1. *Necessary Possibility of Change (L3).* T1 applied to the Cartesian witness yields □◇C. (§2.3)
1. *Structural Requirement.* Necessarily possible change requires the three Conditions. □(◇C → (T∧S∧Φ)). (§2.4)
1. *Triconditional Necessity.* The three Conditions are jointly and necessarily instantiated. □(T∧S∧Φ). (§2.5)
1. *Triconditional Identity (T5).* Within change-realizing structure, the three Conditions form one mutually implicating realizer complex, with Nature naming their necessary co-instantiation. (§2.6)
1. *Nothing Beneath.* No empty alternative lies under that structure. ¬◇∅. (§2.7)
1. *Reality–Nature Identity.* Reality is maximal, every real content is conditioned by Nature, and the Grounding Trilemma leaves no exterior grounding position. Structurally, R = N.
1. **Necessity of Nature (T6).** Therefore any possible Reality is Nature: the necessary co-instantiation of T, S, and Φ, with contingent configurations within it.

:::

Six results unfold that identification, each inheriting the chapter-level closure: the nomological laws are constitutive rather than contingent (§2.8.1), the denial of Nature is self-refuting (§2.8.2), Φ presupposes T and S so the result is not physicalism (§2.8.3), contingency belongs to configurations within Nature rather than to Nature itself (§2.8.4), Nature's necessity is formally stated (§2.8.5), and every rival structural ground is precluded (§2.8.6).

This is not one worldview set beside others to be weighed. It is the terminus of a derivation. T, S, and Φ are not predictions about what fundamental physics will eventually discover but role-level conditions any physics must already presuppose. Their realization as particular temporal metrics, spatial geometries, fields, laws, and material systems remains contingent physical content.

*Scope of the verdict.* The identity reached here is modal and structural: necessarily, any Reality instantiates Nature, and no additional ground occupies a position outside the Conditions. What this chapter does not yet close is the further claim that nothing transcendent stands alongside Nature under every theistic description. The structural form of that preclusion is set out at §2.8.6; its full form is the work of Chapters 5 and 6, and the unconditional verdict that Reality is Nature and nothing besides is not pronounced until Chapter 7, §7.9.[^necessity-of-nature-ch4]

[^necessity-of-nature-ch4]: The Necessity of Nature is challenged across Chapter 4 by idealism (§4.3.5), the Mathematical Universe Hypothesis (§4.3.7), structural realism (§4.3.9), Humean contingency (§4.1.4), and two-dimensional semantics (§4.1.2). The Conceivability Trap (§3.3.4) develops a convergent line, and phenomenal-consciousness objections are carried in Chapter 8.
